voice_profile: Natural mature British male medical teacher. Conversational, thoughtful, unhurried and slightly informal rather than an announcer.

stages.script:
Okay, imagine you are the responsible doctor in A&E.

An eight-year-old boy attends the emergency department with symptoms of pneumonia.

When you take the history, you find that he has been unwell for about three days. He has not been eating or drinking particularly well.

You take some bloods, put a cannula in, and because his oral intake is poor, you start him on intravenous fluids.

He is admitted to the ward.

The following morning, he does not seem quite right.

He is a little sleepy. He complains of a headache. He feels sick.

You repeat his blood tests.

His sodium comes back at:

122 mmol/L.

All right.

That is significant hyponatraemia.

And the question is:

Why?

What has happened in this child that has caused his sodium to fall to 122?

In order to work that out logically, we first need to understand how sodium and water are normally handled in the body.

And actually, for this lecture, we only need three basic ideas.

First idea — serum sodium is a concentration

A normal serum sodium is roughly:

135 to 145 mmol/L.

But what does that actually mean?

When we measure sodium in the blood, we are not measuring how much sodium the body contains in total.

We are measuring a concentration.

The unit is millimoles per litre.

A mole is simply a way of counting particles, and a millimole is one-thousandth of a mole.

For this lecture, though, you do not need to worry too much about the chemistry.

The important bit is:

per litre.

We are talking about how much sodium is present relative to a certain volume of water.

So if the sodium concentration becomes low, there are really only a few broad possibilities.

You may have lost sodium.

You may have gained water.

Or both things may have happened together.

And that distinction is going to become very important.

Second idea — the body is very good at holding onto sodium

If circulating volume falls, the kidney detects that something is wrong.

This activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.

We will cover that properly in the Fundamentals section, because the full mechanism is more detailed than we need here.

But for now, the important endpoint is simple.

Aldosterone tells the kidney:

keep sodium.

So if sodium intake falls, or if a child starts losing sodium, the kidney will normally try very hard to reduce further sodium loss.

It reabsorbs more sodium and reduces the amount of sodium appearing in the urine.

That is why poor sodium intake on its own rarely causes severe hyponatraemia.

It may contribute, particularly in an unwell child, but usually something else is happening as well.

Explore deeper: Renin–Angiotensin–Aldosterone System

Third idea — ADH controls water

Now we need to look at water.

ADH stands for:

antidiuretic hormone.

It is also called vasopressin.

ADH is produced by neurons in the hypothalamus and then transported to the posterior pituitary, where it is stored and released into the bloodstream.

There are two particularly important reasons why ADH is released.

The first is when the blood becomes too concentrated.

The hypothalamus senses an increase in plasma osmolality and responds by releasing ADH.

The message is essentially:

we need to keep water.

The second important trigger is a fall in effective circulating volume.

If the circulation is poorly filled, the body will also increase ADH release.

And that becomes very important in hyponatraemia.

ADH travels to the kidney and acts mainly on the collecting ducts.

It binds to V2 receptors and causes water channels called aquaporin-2 channels to be inserted into the cell membrane.

That allows more water to move out of the tubular fluid and back into the circulation.

So:

more ADH means more water retained.

Less ADH means more water excreted.

ADH can also rise in response to things such as:

- nausea
- pain
- stress
- pulmonary disease
- central nervous system disease

And that should already make you think again about our child with pneumonia.

Explore deeper: ADH and Water Balance

So before we go back to the case

There are only three things I want you to remember.

One: serum sodium is a concentration.

Two: aldosterone helps the body retain sodium.

Three: ADH helps the body retain water.

Now we can go back to our eight-year-old with pneumonia and a sodium of 122 and ask the real question:

Has he lost sodium?

Has he gained water?

Is he retaining water because ADH is active?

Or are several of these things happening at the same time?

That is how we are going to approach his hyponatraemia.

So where can sodium actually be lost from?

Let’s start with the most obvious possibility.

Could the child simply not be taking enough sodium in?

He has not been eating particularly well for three days.

Could that explain a sodium of 122?

Usually not.

And the reason is that the kidney is very good at conserving sodium.

If sodium intake falls, aldosterone and the rest of the sodium-retaining systems reduce urinary sodium losses dramatically.

So poor intake may contribute, but by itself it usually does not explain severe hyponatraemia.

So now we look at actual sodium loss.

There are several important routes.

Gastrointestinal sodium loss

Sodium can be lost through the gastrointestinal tract.

That could be through:

- vomiting
- diarrhoea
- high-output stomas, especially ileostomies
- nasogastric aspiration
- other significant gastrointestinal drainage

All of those fluids contain water and electrolytes, including sodium.

If enough is lost, the child loses extracellular volume.

And once that circulating volume starts to fall, ADH rises.

So already you can see how two mechanisms start to interact.

The child is losing sodium.

At the same time, the body is retaining water.

And if we then replace those losses mainly with water or a very hypotonic fluid, the sodium concentration can fall even further.

So in a child with hyponatraemia, ask:

Have they been vomiting?

Have they had diarrhoea?

Do they have an ileostomy?

Are we aspirating large volumes through an NG tube?

And then ask:

What have those losses been replaced with?

Renal sodium loss

The second major route is the kidney.

Normally, if the body is short of sodium or volume depleted, the kidney should conserve sodium very aggressively.

So if the child is still losing a lot of sodium in the urine, we need to ask why.

One obvious cause is medication.

Diuretics are designed to make the kidney excrete sodium.

Water follows sodium.

So a child receiving a diuretic can lose both sodium and water.

There are also renal tubular disorders and salt-wasting nephropathies.

In these conditions, the renal tubules are unable to reabsorb sodium properly.

So sodium continues to appear in the urine even when the body would prefer to retain it.

And then there are hormonal causes.

Adrenal insufficiency is important.

Aldosterone normally promotes sodium reabsorption.

If aldosterone activity is deficient, sodium can be lost in the urine.

And adrenal insufficiency can produce hyponatraemia through more than one mechanism, because cortisol deficiency can also increase ADH release.

So the child can lose sodium and retain water at the same time.

Another important cause, particularly in children with intracranial disease or after neurosurgery, is cerebral salt wasting.

Here the kidney loses sodium in association with neurological disease.

The child becomes volume depleted.

And because the child becomes volume depleted, ADH rises.

Again, several mechanisms interact.

Sodium loss through the skin

Sodium can also be lost through the skin.

Usually this is relatively small, but it can become important with:

- large burns
- very heavy sweating
- prolonged heat exposure
- extensive exudative skin disease

Sweat contains sodium.

Burns can lead to substantial fluid and electrolyte loss through damaged skin.

Other external fluid losses

There are also less common situations where sodium-containing fluid is being lost from the body.

For example:

- surgical drains
- fistulae
- pancreatic drainage
- biliary drainage
- large-volume pleural drainage
- abdominal drainage

The exact electrolyte content depends on the fluid involved, but the general principle is the same.

If sodium-containing extracellular fluid is leaving the body, total body sodium can fall.

So what is our first clinical question?

It is actually very simple.

Has this child been losing fluid somewhere?

If yes:

Where from?

Then:

What is in that fluid?

And finally:

What have we replaced it with?

That last question is often just as important as the first.

But sodium may be low even if sodium has not been lost

Now we come to the other major mechanism.

Remember:

serum sodium is a concentration.

You can lower a concentration either by removing sodium or by adding water.

So a child can become hyponatraemic because there is simply too much water relative to the amount of sodium present.

This is dilutional hyponatraemia.

And this is where ADH becomes central.

Why would the body retain water?

Normally, if the plasma becomes dilute, ADH should switch off.

The kidney should produce very dilute urine and get rid of free water.

So if a child is hyponatraemic and the kidney is still producing concentrated urine, something is driving ADH.

The question then becomes:

why is ADH active?

There are several reasons.

One is volume depletion.

If the child has lost fluid through diarrhoea, vomiting or renal salt wasting, ADH may be entirely appropriate.

The body is prioritising circulation over osmolality.

Another is nausea or pain.

These are very potent non-osmotic triggers of ADH.

Another is pulmonary disease.

And this is where our pneumonia becomes relevant.

Pneumonia can trigger inappropriate or non-osmotic ADH release.

Central nervous system disease can do the same.

And some medications can stimulate ADH or increase its effect.

SIADH

Now we come to SIADH.

The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion.

The basic problem is that ADH is active when, from an osmotic point of view, it should not be.

The plasma is already dilute.

The sodium is already low.

And yet the kidney continues to retain water.

So the urine remains relatively concentrated.

Common causes include:

- pulmonary disease
- CNS disease
- pain
- nausea
- postoperative states
- some medications

In paediatrics, pulmonary infections and CNS disease are particularly relevant.

But why does SIADH not usually cause massive oedema?

That is a useful question.

If ADH keeps water, why do these patients not simply become more and more overloaded?

Initially, there is some water retention.

That causes a small expansion in extracellular volume.

The body responds by suppressing renin and aldosterone and increasing sodium excretion.

So sodium is lost in the urine.

Eventually, the patient reaches a sort of new equilibrium.

They have retained water, but they are not usually dramatically oedematous.

Clinically, they appear roughly euvolaemic.

That is why SIADH is classically described as euvolaemic hyponatraemia.

Before calling something SIADH

There are a few conditions that can look very similar.

One important one is adrenal insufficiency.

Cortisol normally suppresses ADH.

If cortisol is deficient, ADH rises.

So a patient with cortisol deficiency can look biochemically very similar to SIADH.

Severe hypothyroidism can also contribute to hyponatraemia.

So SIADH is not simply:

low sodium plus concentrated urine.

It is a diagnosis that has to make sense in context.

The next important concept — osmolality

Before we decide what type of hyponatraemia this is, we need to know whether the plasma is actually hypotonic.

Usually it is.

But not always.

Plasma osmolality tells us how concentrated the plasma is overall.

So when we see hyponatraemia, there are three broad possibilities.

Hypotonic hyponatraemia

This is the common and clinically important form.

The sodium is low and the plasma osmolality is low.

This means the extracellular fluid really is dilute.

This is the group where our sodium-and-water framework applies most directly.

Hypertonic hyponatraemia

The classic example is severe hyperglycaemia.

Glucose accumulates in the extracellular space.

It pulls water out of cells.

That extra extracellular water dilutes the sodium.

So the measured sodium falls.

But the plasma is not hypotonic.

It may actually be hypertonic.

So in severe hyperglycaemia, we need to think about the corrected sodium rather than reacting blindly to the measured value.

Pseudohyponatraemia

This is much less common.

Very high lipid or protein concentrations can interfere with some laboratory methods and produce an apparently low sodium even though plasma water sodium is actually normal.

The key point is simply:

not every low sodium is true hypotonic hyponatraemia.

So check the osmolality and the clinical context.

Now assume this is true hypotonic hyponatraemia

At this point, one of the most useful tests is:

urine osmolality.

And the logic is simple.

If the plasma is already too dilute, ADH should normally be suppressed.

So the kidney should be producing very dilute urine.

If the urine is very dilute, the kidney is doing what it should.

If the urine is concentrated, ADH is active.

That gives us a major branch point in the diagnostic pathway.

Very dilute urine

If the urine osmolality is below roughly 100 mOsm/kg, ADH is largely suppressed.

The kidney is trying to get rid of water.

So if the child is still hyponatraemic, think about situations where water intake exceeds the kidney's excretory capacity or where there is very low solute intake.

Examples include:

- excessive water intake
- very low solute intake
- occasionally large volumes of hypotonic fluid

Concentrated urine

If the urine osmolality is clearly elevated, ADH is active.

Now the question is:

why?

And this is where volume status becomes important.

The three volume states

Traditionally, we divide hypotonic hyponatraemia into:

- hypovolaemic
- euvolaemic
- hypervolaemic

It is not perfect.

Clinical volume assessment can be difficult.

But it is very useful physiologically.

Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia

Imagine a child with severe diarrhoea.

They lose sodium and water.

Circulating volume falls.

ADH rises.

The child becomes thirsty.

If they then replace the losses mainly with plain water, or receive very hypotonic fluid, the sodium can fall markedly.

So this child has:

sodium depletion

plus

water retention driven by ADH.

That is why simply restricting water would be wrong.

The primary problem is hypovolaemia.

Restore the circulation appropriately, and the stimulus for ADH falls.

The kidney can then begin to excrete free water again.

Urinary sodium in hypovolaemia

Urinary sodium can help.

If the body is volume depleted and the kidneys are functioning appropriately, they should be trying desperately to retain sodium.

So the urinary sodium should generally be low.

That suggests extrarenal losses such as:

- vomiting
- diarrhoea
- stoma losses
- skin losses

If the child is volume depleted but the urine sodium remains high, think about renal sodium loss.

That includes:

- diuretics
- adrenal insufficiency
- renal tubular disorders
- cerebral salt wasting

The exact cut-off is less important than the principle:

is the kidney conserving sodium, or is it wasting sodium?

Euvolaemic hyponatraemia

This is where SIADH sits.

The patient does not look frankly dehydrated.

They do not have obvious oedema.

They look roughly euvolaemic.

The plasma is hypotonic.

The urine is inappropriately concentrated.

And the urinary sodium is usually not low.

That pattern should make you think of SIADH, but only once adrenal and other relevant causes have been considered.

Hypervolaemic hyponatraemia

Now imagine a patient with obvious excess total body fluid.

They may have:

- oedema
- ascites
- pulmonary oedema

And yet the sodium is low.

This happens in conditions such as:

- heart failure
- advanced renal failure
- severe liver disease
- some nephrotic states

The key concept is effective circulating volume.

The body may contain too much fluid overall, but the arterial circulation may still be underfilled from the body's point of view.

So ADH remains active.

Water retention continues.

And the sodium concentration falls.

SIADH versus cerebral salt wasting

This is particularly important in neurology and neurosurgery.

Both can produce:

- low sodium
- low plasma osmolality
- concentrated urine
- high urinary sodium

So the laboratory results can look surprisingly similar.

But the physiology is different.

In SIADH, the primary problem is water retention.

The patient is generally euvolaemic.

In cerebral salt wasting, the primary problem is renal sodium loss.

The patient becomes hypovolaemic.

That means the clinical context matters enormously.

Look at:

- weight trend
- urine output
- fluid balance
- perfusion
- blood pressure
- signs of dehydration

A child with high urine output, falling weight and negative fluid balance is very different from a child who is clinically euvolaemic and retaining water.

And the treatment is different as well.

Why hyponatraemia causes neurological symptoms

Now let’s come back to the headache and sleepiness in our original child.

Why does low sodium affect the brain?

Because sodium is a major determinant of extracellular tonicity.

If extracellular sodium falls, extracellular fluid becomes more dilute.

Water then moves into cells.

That includes brain cells.

The brain swells.

And unlike many other tissues, the brain is trapped inside a rigid skull.

So swelling can increase intracranial pressure.

Symptoms can include:

- headache
- nausea
- vomiting
- confusion
- drowsiness
- seizures
- coma

The severity depends not just on how low the sodium is, but also on how quickly it fell.

Acute versus chronic hyponatraemia

If sodium falls quickly, the brain has little time to adapt.

So acute hyponatraemia is particularly dangerous.

If the sodium has been low for longer, the brain adapts.

Brain cells begin to lose intracellular electrolytes and organic osmolytes.

Water follows.

That reduces swelling.

But that adaptation creates a second danger.

If chronic hyponatraemia is corrected too quickly, the extracellular compartment becomes relatively hypertonic.

Water is pulled out of the adapted brain cells.

They shrink.

That can lead to osmotic demyelination syndrome.

So there are two opposite dangers:

too rapid a fall in sodium can cause cerebral oedema

and

too rapid a correction of chronic hyponatraemia can cause osmotic demyelination.

What if the child is seizing?

Now imagine our child deteriorates and has a seizure.

At that point, this is an emergency.

The immediate problem is cerebral oedema.

You do not wait for every diagnostic test to come back.

You need to raise extracellular tonicity enough to reverse the neurological symptoms.

That means hypertonic saline according to the local paediatric emergency protocol.

The goal is not to restore sodium to 140 immediately.

The goal is to raise it enough to treat the acute neurological emergency.

After that, correction becomes slower and carefully controlled.

What if the child is not severely symptomatic?

Then management depends on the cause.

If the child is hypovolaemic:

restore circulating volume appropriately and treat the source of the loss.

If this is SIADH:

remove the trigger where possible and restrict free water.

If this is adrenal insufficiency:

replace glucocorticoid and manage the associated volume and electrolyte disturbance.

If this is cerebral salt wasting:

replace sodium and volume.

If this is a fluid-overloaded state:

treat the underlying cardiac, renal or hepatic problem and manage water balance.

So there is no single treatment called:

treatment of sodium 122.

You treat the physiology that produced the sodium of 122.

Let’s test the reasoning

A ten-year-old child with meningitis has:

- sodium 124 mmol/L
- low plasma osmolality
- urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg
- urinary sodium 75 mmol/L

What is the diagnosis?

You cannot answer yet.

You need one more piece of information.

What is the volume status?

Suppose the child has:

- stable weight
- normal perfusion
- normal urine output
- approximately balanced fluid input and output

SIADH becomes very plausible.

Now change the picture.

The child has:

- urine output of 6 mL/kg/hour
- falling weight
- negative fluid balance
- tachycardia
- dry mucous membranes

Same sodium.

Same urine osmolality.

Same high urine sodium.

But now the physiology points towards cerebral salt wasting.

That is why you cannot diagnose hyponatraemia from one laboratory result.

A practical approach

So let’s put the whole thing into a sequence you can actually use.

Step one

Is the child severely symptomatic?

Look for:

- seizures
- markedly reduced consciousness
- severe neurological symptoms

If yes, treat urgently.

Step two

Is this true hypotonic hyponatraemia?

Check plasma osmolality.

Look at glucose.

Consider pseudohyponatraemia if the context suggests it.

Step three

What is the urine osmolality?

If the urine is very dilute:

ADH is suppressed.

If the urine is concentrated:

ADH is active.

Step four

Why is ADH active?

Assess the volume state.

Is the child:

- hypovolaemic
- euvolaemic
- hypervolaemic

Step five

What is the kidney doing with sodium?

Look at urinary sodium.

Is the kidney conserving sodium?

Or is it losing sodium?

Step six

What is the underlying cause?

Think about:

- gastrointestinal losses
- renal losses
- diuretics
- adrenal insufficiency
- SIADH
- cerebral salt wasting
- renal disease
- cardiac disease
- liver disease
- excessive water intake
- IV fluids
- medications
- CNS disease
- pulmonary disease

And then treat the mechanism.

Now go back to our original child

We have an eight-year-old with pneumonia.

He has had poor oral intake.

He has been started on intravenous fluids.

The next day he has:

- headache
- nausea
- drowsiness
- sodium 122 mmol/L

So what might be happening?

Poor intake by itself is unlikely to explain this.

We need to know:

Has he been vomiting?

Has he had diarrhoea?

What intravenous fluid has he received?

How much?

What is his fluid balance?

What is his weight trend?

What is his urine output?

What is his plasma osmolality?

What is his urine osmolality?

What is his urinary sodium?

If the plasma osmolality is low, the urine is concentrated, he is clinically euvolaemic and the urinary sodium is not low, then SIADH related to his pneumonia becomes very plausible.

The pneumonia provides a non-osmotic stimulus for ADH.

ADH acts on the collecting duct.

Aquaporin channels are inserted.

The kidney retains water.

The intravenous fluid adds additional water.

Water accumulates relative to sodium.

The plasma sodium concentration falls.

The extracellular fluid becomes hypotonic.

Water moves into brain cells.

And that explains the headache, nausea and drowsiness.

Now the whole case fits together.

Final reconstruction

Let’s finish by rebuilding the mechanism from beginning to end.

Pneumonia

causes increased non-osmotic ADH release.

ADH travels to the kidney.

It binds to V2 receptors in the collecting duct.

Aquaporin-2 channels are inserted.

More water is reabsorbed.

The child is also receiving intravenous fluid.

Water accumulates relative to sodium.

The sodium concentration falls.

Plasma tonicity falls.

Water moves into cells.

Brain cells swell.

The child develops headache, nausea and drowsiness.

And if the process becomes severe enough:

seizures and reduced consciousness can follow.

That is hyponatraemia understood as physiology rather than memorised as a list.

Take-home points

If you remember only a few things, remember these.

Serum sodium is a concentration, not a measure of total body sodium.

Hyponatraemia can result from sodium loss, water gain, or both.

Aldosterone helps the kidney retain sodium.

ADH helps the kidney retain water.

If plasma is hypotonic, the kidney should normally produce dilute urine.

Concentrated urine means ADH is active — then ask why.

Volume status helps distinguish hypovolaemic, euvolaemic and hypervolaemic causes.

Urinary sodium helps tell you whether the kidney is conserving sodium or wasting it.

Acute severe hyponatraemia can cause cerebral oedema.

Chronic hyponatraemia must not be corrected too quickly because of the risk of osmotic demyelination.

And most importantly:

do not treat the sodium number in isolation. Treat the mechanism that produced it.
